The Highland Clearances. A systematic removal of tenant farmers and crofters from the Scottish Highlands between roughly 1760 and 1850. Landlords transformed communal clan lands into privately owned estates used for sheep ranching, driven by economic rationalization and agricultural improvement ideology, and enabled by the dismantling of the clan system following the Jacobite defeat in 1746. The Clearances displaced tens of thousands, fundamentally reshaped the geography, demography, and social structure of the Highlands, and triggered mass emigration to North America, Australia, and other colonies.

The clearances followed the suppression of the Jacobite clans in 1746, an event that had already destabilized the Highlands' traditional feudal social order. Landlords became less interested in their obligations to tenants and more focused on profit. They enclosed common lands and removed tenant farmers to create unified sheep-ranching estates, applying an ideology of "improvement" that prioritized capitalist efficiency over community continuity. The displacement affected primarily the far north—Sutherland, Ross and Cromarty—and the Hebridean islands, where entire glens were emptied of human population within a single generation.

The timing overlapped with the Industrial Revolution, when Lowland Scotland industrialized rapidly. The Highlands were economized into a rural periphery, their resources devoted to serving urban industrial needs. The result was mass emigration: an estimated forty-six thousand Scots emigrated to North America and Australia during the Clearances, establishing diaspora communities and exporting Highland grievance internationally. Depopulation was severe—the Highlands' share of Scotland's population fell from roughly forty percent in 1700 to less than ten percent by 1900, an absolute decline with lasting cultural consequences that reverberate in Scottish identity to this day.
